title: Olympiad angle chasing
blurb: Cyclic quadrilaterals, directed angles and the standard configurations, used to write complete synthetic proofs.
outcomes: Prove and use the converses of the cyclic and tangent criteria
Run an angle chase with directed angles that works in every configuration
Recognise orthocentre, antiparallel and incentre-excentre configurations and write BMO-standard proofs
lesson:
In an acute triangle $ABC$ with orthocentre $H$, the reflection of $H$ in $BC$ lies on the circumcircle. To prove this, let $BE$ and $CF$ be altitudes. The right angles at $E$ and $F$ put $A,F,H,E$ on a circle (the circle with diameter $AH$), so $\angle BHC=\angle FHE=180^\circ-\angle A$. The reflection $H'$ satisfies $\angle BH'C=\angle BHC=180^\circ-\angle A$ and lies on the opposite side of $BC$ from $A$, so the opposite angles of $ABH'C$ add to $180^\circ$, so $ABH'C$ is cyclic. This lemma is worth remembering, and we use the lemma again in Example 4.

The proof used right angles to get a circle, read an angle off that circle, and used the angle to get a second circle. Most olympiad angle chases alternate in this way between angle equalities and concyclicities. This unit covers the converses that make each step valid, directed angles to handle every configuration with one argument, the standard configurations, and what a marker expects in a written proof.

Criteria and their converses

Cyclic criteria. Four points $A,B,C,D$, no three collinear, are concyclic if and only if either of the following holds. Either $\angle ABD=\angle ACD$ with $B,C$ on the same side of $AD$, or $\angle ABC+\angle ADC=180^\circ$ with $B,D$ on opposite sides of $AC$.

Tangent criterion. A line $t$ through $A$ touches circle $ABC$ if and only if the angle between $t$ and chord $AB$ equals $\angle ACB$, the angle in the alternate segment.

Right angles. $\angle APB=90^\circ$ if and only if $P$ lies on the circle with diameter $AB$.

The forward directions are fairly trivial (the inscribed angle theorem). The method relies on the converses, and they follow from one observation. Fix the segment $AD$ and a circle $\Gamma$ through $A$ and $D$. If $P$ is inside $\Gamma$ (on a given side of $AD$), extend $AP$ to meet the arc at $P'$. Then $\angle APD$ is an exterior angle of triangle $PP'D$, so $\angle APD>\angle AP'D$. A point outside sees $AD$ at a smaller angle in the same way. So on one side of $AD$, the points seeing $AD$ at the angle given by the arc are exactly the points of that arc.

Directed angles

The weakness of these criteria is the side conditions. In a real problem a point may sit on a segment or beyond the segment, and the chase that says $\angle ABC+\angle ADC=180^\circ$ in one picture says $\angle ABC=\angle ADC$ in another. We avoid this by measuring angles between lines, modulo $180^\circ$.

Directed angles. For lines $\ell,m$, let $\measuredangle(\ell,m)$ be the angle through which $\ell$ must be turned anticlockwise to become parallel to $m$, taken modulo $180^\circ$, and write $\measuredangle ABC=\measuredangle(BA,BC)$. Then $\measuredangle(\ell,m)=-\measuredangle(m,\ell)$, $\measuredangle(\ell,m)+\measuredangle(m,n)=\measuredangle(\ell,n)$, $A,B,C$ are collinear iff $\measuredangle ABC=0$, and $\measuredangle ABC+\measuredangle BCA+\measuredangle CAB=0$ in every triangle.

Cyclic criterion. $A,B,C,D$ are concyclic iff $\measuredangle ABC=\measuredangle ADC$. Tangent criterion. $t$ touches circle $ABC$ at $A$ iff $\measuredangle(t,AB)=\measuredangle ACB$.

The directed cyclic criterion covers both cases. If $B$ and $D$ are on the same side of $AC$, triangles $ABC$ and $ADC$ have the same orientation, the directed angles are the ordinary ones with the same sign, and we recover equal angles. If they are on opposite sides, the orientations differ, say $\measuredangle ABC=\angle ABC$ and $\measuredangle ADC=-\angle ADC$, and equality modulo $180^\circ$ means $\angle ABC+\angle ADC=180^\circ$.

Two warnings. First, you cannot halve, because $2x=2y$ only gives $x=y$ or $x=y+90^\circ$, so central angles and angle bisectors need care. Route through a tangent instead. Second, directed angles forget which side of a line a point is on, so they cannot prove betweenness or compute "the angle is $40^\circ$". Use them for concyclicity, collinearity, parallels and tangency.

Standard configurations

The orthocentre. With feet $D,E,F$ of the altitudes, the quadrilaterals $AFHE$, $BDHF$, $CEHD$ (diameters $AH,BH,CH$) and $BCEF$, $CAFD$, $ABDE$ (diameters $BC,CA,AB$) are all cyclic. Also $\angle BAH=90^\circ-\angle B=\angle OAC$, so $AH$ and $AO$ are reflections of each other in the bisector of angle $A$.

Antiparallels. If $X$ on line $AB$ and $Y$ on line $AC$ make $B,C,Y,X$ concyclic, then $\measuredangle(XY,AB)=\measuredangle YXB=\measuredangle YCB=\measuredangle ACB$, which is the angle the tangent at $A$ makes with $AB$. So $XY$ is parallel to that tangent, hence perpendicular to $AO$.

Incentre-excentre lemma. Let line $AI$ meet the circumcircle again at $M$, where $I$ is the incentre and $I_A$ the $A$-excentre. Then $MB=MC=MI=MI_A$.

Proof. $M$ is the midpoint of arc $BC$, so $MB=MC$ and $\angle MBC=\angle MAC=\tfrac12\angle A$. Hence $\angle MBI=\tfrac12\angle A+\tfrac12\angle B$, and $\angle MIB$, an exterior angle of triangle $ABI$, is also $\tfrac12\angle A+\tfrac12\angle B$. So $MB=MI$. The internal and external bisectors at $B$ are perpendicular, so triangle $IBI_A$ has a right angle at $B$, and the only point of the hypotenuse $II_A$ equidistant from $B$ and $I$ is its midpoint, so $M$ is that midpoint and $MI_A=MI$.

Worked examples

Example 1. Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with circumcentre $O$, and let $D$ be the foot of the altitude from $A$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $D$ to $AB$ and $AC$. Prove that $XY\perp AO$.

One could compute lengths such as $AX=AD^2/AB$, but an angle chase is shorter. Since $\angle AXD=\angle AYD=90^\circ$, the points $X$ and $Y$ lie on the circle with diameter $AD$, so

\[\angle AYX=\angle ADX=90^\circ-\angle DAB=\angle ABC.\]

So $B,C,Y,X$ are concyclic (exterior angle equals interior opposite angle), and by the antiparallel fact $XY\perp AO$. To finish by hand instead, note that triangle $AOC$ is isosceles with apex angle $2\angle B$, so $\angle OAC=90^\circ-\angle B$. If $AO$ meets $XY$ at $T$, triangle $ATY$ has angles $90^\circ-\angle B$ at $A$ and $\angle B$ at $Y$, leaving $90^\circ$ at $T$.

Note that two right angles subtending a common segment give a circle on that segment as diameter (here the circle with diameter $AD$), and angles can then be transferred through that circle. You should look for such pairs before anything else.

Example 2. $BC$ is a fixed chord of a circle $\omega$, not a diameter, and $A$ moves on $\omega$. The circle through $A$ tangent to line $BC$ at $B$ meets line $AC$ again at $P$, and the circle through $A$ tangent to $BC$ at $C$ meets line $AB$ again at $Q$. Prove that lines $BP$ and $CQ$ pass through a fixed point.

As $A$ moves over both arcs, $P$ can lie on segment $AC$, beyond $A$ or beyond $C$, so an undirected chase would need cases. With directed angles one argument covers all of them.

By the tangent criterion in circle $ABP$, $\measuredangle(BC,BP)=\measuredangle BAP=\measuredangle BAC$, the last step because $P$ lies on line $AC$. (Fixed angles for a moving point.) We look for an angle that does not change as $A$ moves. By the cyclic criterion, $\measuredangle BAC$ is the same for every point $A$ of $\omega$, whichever arc $A$ is on. Call this angle $\theta$. So $BP$ is the line through $B$ at directed angle $\theta$ to $BC$, which is fixed. In the same way $\measuredangle(CB,CQ)=\measuredangle CAB=-\theta$, so $CQ$ is also a fixed line.

Two fixed lines meet at a fixed point unless they are parallel, which needs $2\theta=0$, that is $\angle BAC=90^\circ$ and $BC$ a diameter, which is excluded. The point can be identified. The tangent to $\omega$ at $B$ makes angle $\measuredangle(BC,t_B)=-\theta$, so line $BP$ is its mirror image in $BC$, and likewise for $C$. Hence the fixed point is the reflection in $BC$ of the point $T$ where the tangents at $B$ and $C$ meet.

Example 3. Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB\neq AC$ and incentre $I$. The circle through $B$, $I$, $C$ meets line $AB$ again at $X$ and line $AC$ again at $Y$. Prove that $XY$ is tangent to the incircle.

Chasing gives $\angle AXY=\angle ACB$ quickly, since $B,C,Y,X$ are concyclic, but tangency is a statement about the distance from $I$ to $XY$, which angles at $X$ and $Y$ do not determine, and this is the hard step. Instead we use the incentre-excentre lemma, which says that circle $BIC$ has centre $M$ on line $AI$. A circle centred on a line is symmetric in that line, and reflection in $AI$ swaps lines $AB$ and $AC$.

So the reflection $C^*$ of $C$ in $AI$ lies on the circle and on line $AB$, hence is $B$ or $X$. The point $C^*$ is not $B$, because $AC^*=AC\neq AB$. Thus $X=C^*$ and similarly $Y=B^*$, so line $XY$ is the mirror image of line $BC$. The incircle is its own mirror image and touches $BC$, so the incircle touches $XY$. The argument also shows $AX=AC$ and $AY=AB$.

(Reflection in an axis of symmetry.) When a circle's centre lies on an axis of symmetry of the figure, reflect.

Example 4. Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with circumcentre $O$. The circle through $B$, $O$, $C$ meets lines $AB$ and $AC$ again at $D$ and $E$, different from $B$ and $C$. Prove that the reflection of $O$ in $DE$ lies on the circle through $A$, $D$, $E$.

The conclusion resembles the fact proved at the start of the unit, so we guess that $O$ is the orthocentre of $ADE$, and aim for $DO\perp AE$. Depending on the shape of $ABC$, $D$ may lie on segment $AB$ or beyond $B$, so we use directed angles.

Computing $\measuredangle OCB$ is the hard step. The familiar value $90^\circ-\angle A$ comes from halving $\angle BOC=2\angle A$, which directed angles do not allow. Use the tangent $t$ at $C$ instead. Since $t\perp CO$, \[\measuredangle(CO,CB)=\measuredangle(CO,t)+\measuredangle(t,CB)=90^\circ+\measuredangle CAB.\] Now circle $BOCD$ and the line $ABD$ give \[\measuredangle(DO,AC)=\measuredangle ODB+\measuredangle(AB,AC)=\measuredangle OCB+\measuredangle BAC=90^\circ+\measuredangle CAB+\measuredangle BAC=90^\circ.\]

So $DO\perp AE$, and swapping the roles of $B$ and $C$ gives $EO\perp AD$, so $O$ is the orthocentre of $ADE$. (The triangle is non-degenerate, since $A$ cannot lie on circle $BOC$, as $A$ sees $BC$ at $\angle A$, not $2\angle A$.) To finish without asking whether $ADE$ is acute, redo the opening proof with directed angles. Turning both lines through $90^\circ$ gives $\measuredangle DOE=\measuredangle(AE,AD)=\measuredangle EAD$. Reflection reverses directed angles, so the reflection $O'$ satisfies $\measuredangle DO'E=\measuredangle DAE$, and $A,D,E,O'$ are concyclic.

Writing up the solution

A BMO marker wants a proof that is correct in every configuration and checkable line by line. Say at the start if you use directed angles modulo $180^\circ$. Give a reason for every equality (which circle, which collinearity, which tangent). Prove a concyclicity before you use the circle. Deal with degenerate cases in a sentence. A diagram is a guide, never a justification.

Common traps.

  • Proving the result only for your drawing when a point could lie on a segment or its extension.
  • Halving directed angles, for instance with central angles or bisectors.
  • Using "the points look cyclic" in place of a criterion.
  • Circular reasoning. When the claim is that $P$ lies on a circle, do not draw $P$ on the circle and read off angles. Prove an angle equality, or define $P'$ on the circle and show $P'=P$.
  • Trying to get betweenness or an actual angle size out of directed angles.

How to spot this in a contest

Use these methods when the conclusion is concyclicity, collinearity, parallel or perpendicular lines, or tangency, and the data are angles, right angles, tangents or circles. I would work in the following order.

  1. Mark every right angle and every tangent, since each gives a circle or an angle equality.
  2. If you see an orthocentre, an incentre, an arc midpoint or a circumcentre, recall the standard facts above before chasing.
  3. If the chase stalls, draw an accurate figure, look for four points that seem concyclic but have not been joined yet, and prove that as a lemma (an auxiliary circle).
  4. If a point moves, ask which directed angle stays fixed.

practice.q: Let $ABC$ be a triangle and let $D$ be a point on side $BC$, other than $B$ and $C$. The tangent at $D$ to the circle $ABD$ meets line $AC$ at $E$, and the tangent at $D$ to the circle $ACD$ meets line $AB$ at $F$. Prove that $EF\parallel BC$.
practice.hint: First show that $A$, $E$, $D$, $F$ are concyclic, by computing $\measuredangle EDF$ from the two tangents.
practice.sol:
We use directed angles modulo $180^\circ$, since $E$ and $F$ may lie on the sides or on their extensions. Note that $E\neq A$, because the tangent at $D$ meets circle $ABD$ only at $D$, and similarly $F\neq A$.

The tangent criterion in circle $ABD$ and in circle $ACD$ gives \[\measuredangle(DE,BC)=\measuredangle DAB,\qquad \measuredangle(DF,BC)=\measuredangle DAC.\] Subtracting, $\measuredangle EDF=\measuredangle DAB-\measuredangle DAC=\measuredangle(AC,AB)=\measuredangle EAF$, the last step because $E$ lies on $AC$ and $F$ on $AB$. Hence $A$, $E$, $D$, $F$ are concyclic.

Now read the angle at $F$ off this circle. \[\measuredangle(FE,AB)=\measuredangle EFA=\measuredangle EDA=\measuredangle(DE,BC)+\measuredangle(BC,AD)=\measuredangle(AD,AB)+\measuredangle(BC,AD)=\measuredangle(BC,AB).\] So $EF\parallel BC$. $\blacksquare$

Remark. Two tangents at the same point $D$ give two angles at $D$, and their difference is an angle of a quadrilateral through $A$. The circle $AEDF$ is not in the statement, and finding the circle is the main step.

practice.q: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with orthocentre $H$, and let $E$ and $F$ be the feet of the altitudes from $B$ and $C$. A line $\ell$ through $H$, other than $AH$, meets the circle $ABH$ again at $X$ and the circle $ACH$ again at $Y$ (take $X=H$ or $Y=H$ if $\ell$ touches that circle). Prove that the midpoint of $XY$ lies on the circle $AEF$.
practice.hint: Compute the directed angles that lines $XA$ and $YA$ make with $\ell$, using $BH\perp AC$ and $CH\perp AB$.
practice.sol:
We use directed angles modulo $180^\circ$, since $X$ and $Y$ may lie on either side of $H$. As $\ell\neq AH$, neither $X$ nor $Y$ is $A$. Since $X$ lies on circle $ABH$ and $BH\perp AC$, \[\measuredangle(XA,\ell)=\measuredangle AXH=\measuredangle ABH=\measuredangle(AB,AC)+\measuredangle(AC,BH)=\measuredangle(AB,AC)+90^\circ,\] with the tangent criterion in place of the cyclic criterion if $X=H$. In the same way, as $CH\perp AB$, \[\measuredangle(YA,\ell)=\measuredangle ACH=\measuredangle(AC,AB)+90^\circ.\]

So $\measuredangle(XA,\ell)=-\measuredangle(YA,\ell)$. Let $N$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $\ell$, and reflect the figure in line $AN$. The reflection maps $\ell$ to itself and reverses directed angles, so the image of line $AX$ is the line through $A$ at directed angle $-\measuredangle(XA,\ell)$ to $\ell$, which is line $AY$. Hence the reflection maps $X$ to $Y$, and $N$ is the midpoint of $XY$.

Finally $\angle ANH=90^\circ$, or $N=H$, so $N$ lies on the circle with diameter $AH$. The right angles at $E$ and $F$ put $E$ and $F$ on the same circle, which is therefore the circle $AEF$. $\blacksquare$

Remark. The reflections of $H$ in $AB$ and $AC$ lie on the circumcircle, so circles $ABH$ and $ACH$ are the reflections of the circumcircle in $AB$ and $AC$ and have its radius $R$. The sine rule in each gives $AX=2R\sin\angle AHX=2R\sin\angle AHY=AY$, which is the same isosceles triangle seen through lengths.

practice.q: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with no right angle and circumcentre $O$, and let $D$ be a point on side $BC$, other than $B$ and $C$. The perpendicular bisector of $BD$ meets line $AB$ at $P$, and the perpendicular bisector of $CD$ meets line $AC$ at $Q$. Prove that $A$, $P$, $O$, $Q$ are concyclic.
practice.hint: Draw the circle with centre $P$ through $B$ and $D$, and the circle with centre $Q$ through $C$ and $D$. Show that their second common point lies on the circumcircle.
practice.sol:
We use directed angles modulo $180^\circ$. Let $\gamma_P$ be the circle with centre $P$ through $B$ and $D$, and $\gamma_Q$ the circle with centre $Q$ through $C$ and $D$. The tangent $t_B$ to $\gamma_P$ at $B$ is perpendicular to the radius $PB$, that is to $AB$, and likewise the tangent $t_C$ to $\gamma_Q$ at $C$ is perpendicular to $AC$.

Step 1. The circles meet again at a point $Z$ other than $B$, $C$, $D$. Line $DP$ is the reflection of line $BP$ in the perpendicular bisector of $BD$, so $\measuredangle(DP,BC)=\measuredangle(BC,AB)$, and in the same way $\measuredangle(DQ,BC)=\measuredangle(BC,AC)$. If the circles touched at $D$, then $P$, $D$, $Q$ would be collinear and these two angles would be equal, which gives $AB\parallel AC$. So there is a second common point $Z\neq D$. Also $Z\neq B$, since otherwise $Q$ would be equidistant from the three collinear points $B$, $D$, $C$, and similarly $Z\neq C$.

Step 2. $Z$ lies on the circumcircle. The tangent criterion in $\gamma_P$ and in $\gamma_Q$ gives \[\measuredangle BZD=\measuredangle(t_B,BC)=90^\circ+\measuredangle(AB,BC),\qquad \measuredangle DZC=\measuredangle(BC,t_C)=\measuredangle(BC,AC)+90^\circ.\] Adding, $\measuredangle BZC=\measuredangle(AB,AC)=\measuredangle BAC$, so $Z$ lies on circle $ABC$ and $OZ=OB=OC$.

Step 3. The points $O$ and $P$ are both equidistant from $B$ and $Z$, so if $P\neq O$ the line $OP$ is the perpendicular bisector of $BZ$. In the same way $OQ\perp CZ$ if $Q\neq O$. Turning both lines through $90^\circ$, \[\measuredangle POQ=\measuredangle(ZB,ZC)=\measuredangle BAC=\measuredangle PAQ,\] as $P$ lies on $AB$ and $Q$ on $AC$. So $A$, $P$, $O$, $Q$ are concyclic. If $P$ or $Q$ coincides with $A$ or $O$, fewer than four distinct points remain and there is nothing to prove. $\blacksquare$

Remark. A point on the perpendicular bisector of $BD$ is the centre of a circle through $B$ and $D$, so draw that circle (an auxiliary circle). Once $Z$ is on the circumcircle, all three of $O$, $P$, $Q$ are centres of circles through $Z$, and their connecting lines are perpendicular to the common chords.

practice.q: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with incentre $I$ and circumcircle $\omega$, and let line $AI$ meet $\omega$ again at $M$. Let $P$ be a point of $\omega$ other than $A$, $B$, $C$, $M$, and let line $PM$ meet line $BC$ at $X$. Prove that the circle through $P$, $X$, $I$ is tangent to line $AI$.
practice.hint: First prove $MB^2=MX\cdot MP$ by showing that $MB$ touches the circle $BXP$. Then bring in the incentre-excentre lemma.
practice.sol:
We use directed angles modulo $180^\circ$, since $P$ may lie on either arc $BC$. As $M$ is the midpoint of arc $BC$, the tangent to $\omega$ at $M$ is parallel to $BC$, so line $PM$ is not parallel to $BC$ and $X$ exists. Also $X\neq B$ (otherwise $P=B$), $X\neq P$ (as $P$ is not on $BC$), and $I$ is not on line $PM$, since line $MI$ is line $MA$ and $P\neq A$.

Step 1. Since $MB=MC$, triangle $MBC$ is isosceles, so $\measuredangle MBC=\measuredangle BCM=\measuredangle BPM$, the last step in $\omega$. As $X$ lies on $BC$ and on $PM$, this reads $\measuredangle(BM,BX)=\measuredangle BPX$, so by the tangent criterion $MB$ touches the circle $BXP$ at $B$. Hence $M$ lies outside this circle, $X$ and $P$ are on the same ray from $M$, and power of a point gives \[MB^2=MX\cdot MP.\]

Step 2. By the incentre-excentre lemma $MI=MB$, so $MI/MX=MP/MI$. The triangles $MIX$ and $MPI$ share the angle at $M$, so they are similar, with opposite orientations. Hence \[\measuredangle(AI,IX)=\measuredangle MIX=\measuredangle IPM=\measuredangle IPX,\] and by the tangent criterion line $AI$ touches the circle $PXI$ at $I$. $\blacksquare$

Remark. Step 1 is the shooting lemma, $MB^2=MX\cdot MP$ for every chord through the arc midpoint $M$. The incentre-excentre lemma then moves the tangent from $B$ to $I$, and the same proof works with the excentre $I_A$ in place of $I$.

practice.q: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB\neq AC$ and incentre $I$. The incircle touches $BC$ at $D$, and $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$. Let $K$ and $L$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $B$ to line $CI$ and from $C$ to line $BI$. Prove that $D$, $K$, $L$, $M$ are concyclic.
practice.hint: Find a circle through $B$, $D$, $I$, $K$ and show that $BC$ bisects angle $KDL$. Then use $MK=ML$.
practice.sol:
We use directed angles modulo $180^\circ$. Since $\angle BIC=90^\circ+\tfrac12\angle A$ is not a right angle, $K\neq I$ and $L\neq I$, and $K\neq L$. As $\angle BCI=\tfrac12\angle C$ is acute, $K$ lies on ray $CI$ and differs from $C$, so $K$ is on the same side of $BC$ as $A$, and the same holds for $L$.

Step 1. $BC$ bisects angle $KDL$. The right angles $\angle BDI=\angle BKI=90^\circ$ put $D$ and $K$ on the circle with diameter $BI$, so \[\measuredangle(DK,BC)=\measuredangle KDB=\measuredangle KIB=\measuredangle(CI,BI).\] In the same way $D$ and $L$ lie on the circle with diameter $CI$, and $\measuredangle(DL,BC)=\measuredangle LDC=\measuredangle LIC=\measuredangle(BI,CI)$. So $\measuredangle(DK,BC)=-\measuredangle(DL,BC)$, and lines $DK$ and $DL$ are reflections of each other in $BC$. These lines are different, because a line equal to its own reflection is $BC$ or perpendicular to $BC$, while $\measuredangle(CI,BI)$ is neither $0$ nor $90^\circ$. Let $\Gamma$ be the circle $DKL$.

Step 2. A phantom point. Let line $BC$ meet $\Gamma$ again at $M'$, with $M'=D$ if $BC$ touches $\Gamma$. Then \[\measuredangle KLM'=\measuredangle KDM'=\measuredangle(DK,BC)=\measuredangle(BC,DL)=\measuredangle M'DL=\measuredangle M'KL,\] using the tangent criterion for the first and last steps when $M'=D$. In triangle $KLM'$ these are the angles at $L$ and $K$, both measured in the sense of the triangle's orientation, so they are equal as ordinary angles and $M'K=M'L$.

Step 3. The right angles $\angle BKC=\angle BLC=90^\circ$ put $K$ and $L$ on the circle with diameter $BC$, so $MK=ML$. Thus $M$ and $M'$ both lie on line $BC$ and on the perpendicular bisector of $KL$. If these two lines did not meet in a single point, $KL$ would be a chord perpendicular to the diameter $BC$, and $BC$ would bisect the chord, putting $K$ and $L$ on opposite sides of $BC$. So $M=M'$, and $M$ lies on $\Gamma$. $\blacksquare$

Remark. Step 2 is the lemma that the bisector of an angle of a triangle and the perpendicular bisector of the opposite side meet on the circumcircle. The hypothesis $AB\neq AC$ only keeps $M\neq D$.

practice.q: Let $ABC$ be a triangle, and let $W$ be a point on line $BC$ other than $B$ and $C$. The circle through $W$ tangent to line $AB$ at $B$ and the circle through $W$ tangent to line $AC$ at $C$ meet again at $X$. Prove that, as $W$ varies, line $WX$ passes through a fixed point.
practice.hint: Show that $X$ lies on the circumcircle. Then look at $\measuredangle BXW$, which does not depend on $W$.
practice.sol:
We use directed angles modulo $180^\circ$, since $W$ may lie on segment $BC$ or outside, and $X$ then moves between the two arcs $BC$. Let $\gamma_B$ and $\gamma_C$ be the two circles and $\omega$ the circumcircle of $ABC$.

First, $X$ exists and differs from $W$, $B$ and $C$. The tangents at the two ends of a chord are reflections of each other in the perpendicular bisector of the chord. So if $\gamma_B$ and $\gamma_C$ touched at $W$ with common tangent $t$, the chord $BW$ of $\gamma_B$ would give $\measuredangle(t,BC)=-\measuredangle(AB,BC)$, the chord $CW$ of $\gamma_C$ would give $\measuredangle(t,BC)=-\measuredangle(AC,BC)$, and $AB\parallel AC$ would follow. Also line $BC$ meets $\gamma_C$ only at $C$ and $W$, so $B\notin\gamma_C$ and $X\neq B$, and similarly $X\neq C$.

Step 1. $X$ lies on $\omega$. The tangent criterion in $\gamma_B$ and in $\gamma_C$ gives \[\measuredangle BXW=\measuredangle(AB,BC),\qquad \measuredangle WXC=\measuredangle(BC,AC).\] Adding, $\measuredangle BXC=\measuredangle(AB,AC)=\measuredangle BAC$, so $X$ lies on $\omega$.

Step 2. The fixed point. Let $Y$ be the point where the line through $A$ parallel to $BC$ meets $\omega$ again, with $Y=A$ if this line touches $\omega$ (that is, if $AB=AC$). Note $Y\neq B$. If $X=Y$ there is nothing to prove. Otherwise the cyclic criterion in $\omega$, or the tangent criterion at $A$ when $Y=A$, gives \[\measuredangle BXY=\measuredangle BAY=\measuredangle(AB,BC),\] since $AY\parallel BC$. Comparing with Step 1, $\measuredangle BXY=\measuredangle BXW$, so $X$, $Y$, $W$ are collinear. Hence every line $WX$ passes through $Y$, the reflection of $A$ in the perpendicular bisector of $BC$. $\blacksquare$

Remark. A point $X$ that sees $BC$ at a fixed directed angle runs over a fixed circle, and if line $XW$ makes a fixed directed angle with $XB$, the line passes through a fixed point of that circle. To name the point, read the fixed angle at $A$ instead of at $X$.

ladder.note: Two right angles on a common segment give a circle, then bring in the tangent.
Alternate segment theorem, then an exterior angle of the cyclic quadrilateral.
Show that two angles at L add up to 180 degrees, reading each off a circle.
Angle chasing alone does not finish, so add an auxiliary point that creates an isosceles or equilateral triangle.
Draw the common tangent at the point of contact and chase through the tangent.
Isosceles triangles at B plus inscribed angles, and directed angles avoid case splits.
Arc midpoints give equal angles, so look for a cyclic quadrilateral through P and Q.
Many right angles mean many circles, so prove collinearity by angles.
Bring in the centre of the circle and find a circle through P and the tangency points.
Guess the fixed point from a special position of P, and arc midpoints are centres of circles through incentres.
Reflections make B equidistant from three points, so check whether Q lies on a line through B.
